item.title: A probabilistic model of visual segmentation explains early visual cortical dynamics
item.description:
Relevance: 35% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Tridib K. Biswas, Ruben Coen-Cagli
arXiv:2611.13316v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural dynamics are a central feature of biological neural systems. In the visual cortex, the functional role of neural dynamics is poorly understood, particularly for static stimuli. The statistics of still natural images have long been used by models that successfully predict firing in early visual cortex; those models assume that neurons represent inferences about latent image features, but often ignore the dynamics of said inference. Here, we test if inferential dynamics in images explain visual-cortical dynamics. To do so, we present a biologically plausible model of cortical computation which assumes that the inference of features is coupled with inference about how those features are organized into meaningful parts, a function also known as segmentation. Given an input image, our model iterates between inferring the features and the segments, through recurrence and feedback, thus inducing dynamics in the neural representation of features. For these neural dynamics, we derive theoretical and exact predictions. Our model predicts both gain and variability in evoked responses to natural images, and we show that it captures classical single-neuron experimental findings such as gain dynamics and variability decay during stimulus presentation. The model also predicts that those dynamics are organized around inferred segment structure and more heterogeneous than previously thought, reflecting the complexity of inference for natural scenes. Finally, our analytical formulation provides a clear interpretation of our results. Insights from our normative model could generalize to segmentation problems in other experimental modalities, and help address the cost of inference in artificial networks with iterative computation.

item.title: Representational Atoms in Neural Networks
item.description:
Relevance: 35% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Chenhui Hu, Pengfei Cao, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao
arXiv:2611.14168v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding the internal representations of neural networks and characterizing their relationship with human conceptual structure are two critical questions for elucidating model mechanisms. The former reveals how learned knowledge is organized in internal representations, whereas the latter provides a basis for interpreting these representations through human conceptual structure. Here, we formally define fundamental representational units (FRUs) and establish two evaluation criteria: fidelity and stability. We further prove that threshold-activated sparse autoencoders (TSAEs) can identify FRUs with high fidelity and stability under appropriate conditions, and validate this result through large-scale experiments. Further analyses reveal that FRUs with higher stability exhibit greater monosemanticity and can be composed across layers to recover semantic organization corresponding to human conceptual structure. These results provide a unified framework for defining, evaluating and identifying FRUs in neural networks, and establish a foundation for characterizing the relationship between neural network representations and human conceptual structure.

item.title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs a Logic of Inference
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Zhimin Hu, Chen Jiang, Hanbo Xie, N. Apurva Ratan Murty, Sashank Varma
arXiv:2611.14483v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural networks are increasingly studied not merely as predictive systems, but as complex systems whose internal computations are themselves objects of scientific inquiry. Recent progress in mechanistic interpretability (MI) has made it possible to identify neurons, features, circuits, population structures, and dynamical patterns associated with model behavior. As these tools improve, attention is shifting from what can be observed inside a model to how those observations support mechanistic explanations. We examine the parallel efforts of neuroscience and MI to address this question and identify recurring inferential bottlenecks when inferring mechanisms from complex neural systems. We propose five principles and organize them into a recursive logic for a more rigorous procedure of mechanistic inference. These principles provide a framework that supports scientific discovery in two senses: it helps turn local interpretability findings into cumulative knowledge of mechanisms within models, and it makes those mechanisms sufficiently precise to generate testable hypotheses about domains beyond the models. Evidence beyond MI is ultimately required to establish what model mechanisms reveal about the world.

item.title: What drives the emergence of symbolic mechanisms in large language models?
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Melody Zixuan Li, Taylor Webb
arXiv:2611.13270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work has identified a set of emergent symbolic mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in large language models, but it remains unclear what factors drive the emergence of these mechanisms. To address this question, we trained neural networks from scratch on abstract sequence tasks, varying both architectural and data distributional factors, and investigated the effects of these factors on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms. Using representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses, we first confirmed that transformer-based language models trained from scratch on our task developed symbolic mechanisms. We then found that, across multiple axes of data diversity, greater diversity produced stronger symbolic signatures. Surprisingly, the same signatures emerged in modified transformer architectures and even multilayer perceptrons, indicating that architectural inductive biases are not necessary for the development of symbolic mechanisms. We also observed consistent patterns in an entity-attribute binding task. Together, these findings identify data diversity, not architecture, as the primary driver of emergent symbolic computation in neural networks.

item.title: Geometric determinants of time series learning and attractor stability in closed-loop circuits
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Barri, A., Gurnani, H., Silver, R. A.
Skilled volitional behaviours arise from recurrent circuits, which can sustain structured neural activity in the absence of external drive, through internal feedback. But how such autonomous activity is learned and stability maintained in distributed motor circuits is poorly understood. To investigate the relationship between neural representations and learning we compared a cortex-like recurrent neural network (RNN) and a cortico-cerebellar-like circuit with a feed-forward layer (RNN+FFL), both in a closed-loop configuration. RNN+FFL circuits learned periodic target signals that parameter-matched RNNs could not, due to a failure to form attractor states. Decomposing population activity by frequency, rather than variance, separated the task-relevant and task-irrelevant subspaces. Quantifying their geometric arrangement revealed that the feed-forward layer improved learning and stabilised attractor states by increasing the angles within and between these subspaces. Our results show that task-specific representational geometry is a better predictor of periodic time series learning in recurrent circuits than classical global measures such as dimensionality.

item.title: Interpreting computational mechanism from multi-area neural recordings
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Versteeg, C., Michaels, J. A., Kashefi, M., Vermani, A., Le, T., Pruszynski, J. A., Pandarinath, C.
Distilling computational mechanisms from neural recordings requires disambiguating intrinsic dynamics from external inputs. Here, we introduce Dynamically Interacting Systems (DynISys), a multi-compartment dynamical-systems model that infers per-area dynamics and structured inter-area communication from multi-area spiking activity. DynISys combines neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) latent dynamics with injective latent-to-neural mappings to achieve expressive and trustworthy dynamical inference. When applied to simultaneous dorsal premotor (PMd) and primary motor (M1) recordings from a continuous reaching task, DynISys accurately reconstructs neuronal responses without inventing spurious latent features. Analyzing the model's dynamics reveals putative mechanisms for motor planning and execution, with PMd-to-M1 inputs positioning a stable fixed point in M1 that encodes execution dynamics for the upcoming movement, subsequently evoked by external (non-PMd) inputs. Finally, multi-session DynISys achieves consistent latents when fit to neural recordings spanning multiple days. In summary, DynISys allows distillation of multi-area recordings into an interpretable account of distributed neural computation.

item.title: Recurrent Modular Structure in Spiking Neural Network Reinforcement Learning
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Vikram Ramavarapu, Himanshu Udupi, Ashish Gautam
arXiv:2611.14262v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Biological neural circuits are both modular and recurrent, with dense communities sparsely linked to one another. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) for reinforcement learning are usually feed-forward, and it is unclear how to obtain functional modules in a recurrent SNN or what they buy. In this work, we introduce a class of spiking networks, called Community Recurrent SNNs (CoRe SNNs): recurrent networks partitioned into communities with fixed roles. A controller community receives the stimulus, each action has its own community, and latent communities carry internal state. Spiking activity is then a walk between communities, and the action is the community the walk reaches. All learning is local and three-factor, and the recurrent communities are closer to cortical microcircuits than a feed-forward actor. We compare three regimes for obtaining the communities: dynamic modularity, in which a new learning rule we introduce, Map-STDP, encourages modular structure during learning; partial modularity, in which a stochastic block model (SBM) initialization enforces it partly; and full modularity, in which sealing enforces it fully. On CartPole, across three spiking neuron models, Map-STDP improves learning over the same network without it matches full modularity (sealed communities) on two of the three models, and makes the observed spike walk more compressible. Replacing the feed-forward actor of a TD-STDP actor-critic with recurrent action communities improves on the feed-forward network on CartPole and LunarLander, and matches it on Acrobot. How strongly to enforce modularity depends on the task: full modularity helps most on Acrobot, while on LunarLander the dynamic, partial and full regimes perform alike. Overall, these recurrent modular networks can match or even improve upon feed-forward approaches, with improvements in bio-plausibility and energy efficiency.

item.title: Examining the Impact of Data and Training Methods on Emergent and Subliminal Misalignment
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Baris Askin, Muhammed Ustaomeroglu, Anupam Nayak, Gauri Joshi, Guannan Qu, Carlee Joe-Wong
arXiv:2605.12798v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Post-training a language model can induce surprising behavioral changes far beyond the intended training target. We study two particularly striking examples: emergent misalignment (EM), where fine-tuning on a narrow dataset leads to misaligned behavior in unrelated contexts, and subliminal learning (SL), where a student model inherits a teacher's misalignment through seemingly benign training data. We examine how the training data, evaluation data, and training method shape where and how strongly misalignment transfers between data and models. We characterize the data by the domain of a prompt (its topical context) and its task (the function the model performs), and we build natural-language and synthetic datasets organized as domain-task grids. We find that EM transfers more strongly to prompts that share the task of the fine-tuning data than to prompts that share its domain. In the synthetic setting, tasks that the model has learned well spread misalignment more broadly. For SL, we go beyond SFT (supervised fine-tuning) to off-policy distillation on the teacher's full next-token distribution and, to our knowledge for the first time, on-policy distillation, where the teacher only scores tokens sampled by the student. Misalignment transfers even under on-policy distillation, more strongly than under SFT and at a level comparable to off-policy distillation. Unlike SFT, where the teacher both generates the data and supervises the student, distillation lets us separate the two. With the teacher fixed, the data change how much misalignment the student inherits, but the teacher determines to which domains and tasks it transfers most strongly. Together, these results show how data and training influence the extent and patterns of emergent and subliminal misalignment.

item.title: Similar visual tuning conceals different recovery dynamics in a model of macaque V1
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Xialei Huang, Qingyu Yan, Zheng Bian, Zhuo-Cheng Xiao
arXiv:2611.13692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Biologically detailed neuronal networks can model how brain circuits perform observed functions, but their high computational cost limits the comparisons needed to test biological hypotheses. To address this limitation, we extend a multiscale approach in which responses of small populations of spiking neurons are computed in advance and reused across a larger cortical circuit. In particular, we approximate these local responses by deep neural networks and achieve an estimated acceleration of the order $10^5$ for steady-state evaluation relative to spiking network simulation. Beyond computational acceleration, the smooth deep surrogate of local responses provides derivatives, allowing us to analyze linear stability and to trace how a perturbation in brain activity is transmitted through different pathways. We demonstrate the approach in a model of an input layer of macaque primary visual cortex (V1), testing circuits under visual stimulation and controlled perturbations. We resolve pathway contributions to stability, strong recurrent responses, and slow recovery. Yet different combinations of pathway strengths can support similar responses to visual stimuli while producing different recovery dynamics. Therefore, Steady responses and perturbation recovery place complementary constraints on candidate circuits. Overall, our approach offers efficient evaluation with an interpretable circuit structure, making systematic comparisons across stimuli and biological hypotheses practical.

item.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks: Methods, Frameworks, and Perspectives
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Lorenzo Cirillo, Irene Amerini, Andrea Cavallaro
arXiv:2611.13868v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep neural networks underpin fundamental tasks in a wide range of signal domains, such as image, audio, and language processing. However, their internal mechanisms are notably difficult to interpret. Internal activations are structured signals transformed across layers that may encode a multitude of interdependent relationships, as individual neurons frequently represent multiple underlying concepts. Mechanistic interpretability aims to uncover the internal mechanisms of neural networks by identifying components whose activations are causally responsible for specific behaviors. In such a context, this article provides an overview of advances in mechanistic interpretability for the analysis of causal inference in deep neural networks.

item.title: BrainVista: Modeling Naturalistic Brain Dynamics as Multimodal Next-Token Prediction
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Xuanhua Yin, Runkai Zhao, Lina Yao, Weidong Cai
arXiv:2602.04512v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Naturalistic fMRI offers a time-resolved window into cortical dynamics during continuous multimodal experience, where future brain states are jointly governed by endogenous neural context and exogenous sensory drive. Forecasting such dynamics, however, remains challenging because fast-changing stimulus streams must be reconciled with the sluggish hemodynamic BOLD response, while cortical activity is organized across functionally heterogeneous brain networks. To address these challenges, we introduce BrainVista, a multimodal autoregressive framework for observed-stimulus conditional brain-state forecasting. BrainVista predicts future fMRI states from the history of brain activity and stimulus tokens temporally aligned to each prediction query, enabling autoregressive prediction without access to future ground-truth fMRI states. Recursive rollout provides a within-run predictive test of brain-state evolution under continuing sensory input. Specifically, we combine Network-wise Tokenizers for functionally structured brain representations, a Spatial Mixer Head for cross-network interaction refinement, and Stimulus-to-Brain (S2B) masking to preserve temporally causal stimulus-brain conditioning while preventing future brain-state leakage and stimulus look-ahead. We evaluate BrainVista on Algonauts 2025, CineBrain, and HAD, three large-scale naturalistic fMRI benchmarks, under long-horizon conditional autoregressive forecasting. BrainVista consistently outperforms baselines, improving pattern correlation by 10.8% and 9.4% relative to the strongest baseline on Algonauts 2025 and CineBrain, respectively. Code is available at https://github.com/xuanhuayin/BrainVista.

item.title: Towards full-stack functionalist theories of consciousness: Identifying the functional profile
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Sushrut Thorat, Paras Chopra
arXiv:2609.33366v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Theories of consciousness often explain different pieces of the phenomenon, leaving open how to construct an account of the whole. If consciousness is functional, a basic question is what awareness of a content changes in how a system can use it. We review experiments comparing how information X is used in a process Y with and without awareness of X, while constraining differences in the information available about X. The resulting preliminary functional profile links awareness most clearly to attentional control, with narrower evidence for metacognitive evaluation, while simple feature--location binding and retrieval can persist without awareness. But these associations constrain rather than explain consciousness. A full-stack theory must also account for the structure and manner of presentation of perceptual and affective experience, subject--world organisation, awareness judgments, and problem reports. Attention Schema Theory illustrates a possible bridge: using a functional association to motivate an internal process model, then proposing that its information also underlies awareness and associated reports. Generalising this approach, we propose using both functional and explanatory profiles to guide the abductive construction of candidate process architectures, implementing and intervening on them, and progressively testing and refining them against further evidence.

item.title: An LFP-based characterization of population-level heterogeneity during motor preparation & execution
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
DePass, M., Falaki, A., Quessy, S., Dancause, N., Cos, I.
The goal of the present work is to characterize mesoscale heterogeneity of population-level neural activity in the motor areas during motor preparation and execution using high-frequency local field potentials (HF-LFPs). Understanding the distribution of neural activity at this scale is necessary since ensembles of neural populations underlie most behaviors. HF-LFPs have emerged as a promising signal for such analysis due to their stability and relationship with cortical population dynamics. Here we analyzed HF-LFPs in non-human primates performing a reach-to-grasp task. We quantified three complementary aspects of heterogeneity: variance, latent dimensionality, and directional coherence. Heterogeneity varied by region and neuromotor state, and was specific to the motor behavior being implemented, even in regions exhibiting high correlation. In addition, more heterogeneous activity tended to better encode neuromotor states. Namely, regions and neuromotor states exhibiting higher variance and dimensionality yielded superior motor decoding performance. Further analyses involving low-dimensional linear projections of the signals revealed rich intra-region interactions between ensembles of populations. The present work helps establish intra-region heterogeneity as a multi-faceted and informative measure of neural activity, even on small spatial scales. It also establishes HF-LFPs as an effective signal for capturing complex intra-region dynamics, making it a suitable candidate for multi-region, systems-level analysis.

item.title: Building World Models from Intrinsic Motivation
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Reece Keller, Declan Kutscher, Xaq Pitkow, Aran Nayebi
arXiv:2611.13113v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the absence of extrinsic rewards or task supervision, human behavior is guided by intrinsic motivation---neural signals that drive curiosity, creativity, play, and other essential facets of intelligence. Intrinsic motivation plays an important developmental role in building robust world models that enable generalization and adaptation. Yet existing studies leave open how a broad range of intrinsic motivations interacts with world-model representation learning to support downstream control. This limits our understanding of which intrinsically collected experiences build reusable models. To address these gaps, we integrate 24 intrinsic objectives, including established methods and explicit variants spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency, into a common model-based reinforcement learning framework. We evaluate the world models they build through zero-shot, few-shot, and multi-task control in locomotion, manipulation, and open-ended gaming environments, using three representation-learning strategies: observation reconstruction, latent prediction, and redundancy reduction. Curiosity-driven exploration with observation reconstruction yields the strongest aggregate family profile, although the best individual pairing depends on the experiment. In compositional vision-based tasks, intrinsic motivation derived from both episodic and lifelong novelty---providing a complementary memory to the world model's generic recurrent state---achieves the best zero-shot transfer and few-shot adaptation. These findings motivate designing intrinsic motivation and representation learning jointly. Our results demonstrate world models as a powerful tool for measuring the quality of intrinsically motivated experience, and positions intrinsic motivation as a key ingredient for building world models autonomously.

item.title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Yeyuan Liu
arXiv:2611.14508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function. Such comparisons can confound wiring with how the models are tuned: a connectome fixes who connects to whom, not the excitability, gains or plasticity rates the model also needs, and modellers often tune these until the real-wiring model works. We separate three estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 restricted to physiology consistent with independent data (P3). The biases involved are known in machine learning (under-tuned baselines, inherited weights, winner's curse); we measure what they do to biological conclusions, using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models. Some claims survive every protocol we test: segregated reward and punishment dopamine improves learning, and head-direction topography is required for a persistent bump. Others do not. In the mushroom body, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 under P1 and P2 but loses to it by 0.09 under P3 (95% CIs exclude zero; held-out runs confirm). The verdict is set by the share of alpha'beta' cells among active Kenyon cells, which P1 selects low; at the share implied by imaging (about 44%) the real-wiring model fails to learn, exposing a model inadequacy rather than a deficit of the fly's wiring. In flyvis, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome, which has a constructed solution within 0.07 (median) of the real error, more than a spatially shuffled one in 50 of 50 members; the ranking survives ten-fold longer retraining but depends on the checkpoint at fifty-fold. A credible structural claim needs matched optimisation, data-constrained physiology and a model that still works there.

item.title: Are Causal Neuron Circuits Unique and Transferable?
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
\"Omer Tekin Yavuz (\.Ileti\c{s}im Yaz{\i}l{\i}m)
arXiv:2611.13885v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Interpretability demonstrations often show that intervening on a group of neurons changes a model's answer. A recent example removes an 18-neuron group in Qwen3-32B and the model answers "Simba" instead of "Scar" to a two-hop Lion King riddle. Such a demonstration establishes that the group matters, but not how much of it is necessary, whether other groups could do the same, or whether the effect carries over to other inputs. We ask: when intervening on a group of neurons changes a model's answer, how much of that group is actually necessary? For every selected group we measure all 4,096 subsets of 12 MLP neurons. On a two-alternative capital task (Qwen3-0.6B), zero-ablating 12 selected neurons lowers the answer margin by 27% while random neurons barely change it, yet replacing the same neurons with their values from other questions also barely changes it: their activations are nearly constant across questions, and we find no evidence that they carry question-specific content. On two-hop relation chains, patching 12 neurons with activations from the first-hop question shifts the answer to the bridge entity (from Scar to Simba): the greedy answer starts with the bridge in 9/11 chains for Qwen3-1.7B, 9/11 for Llama-3.2-1B and 8/10 for Gemma-3-1B; random neurons never do. The full group is rarely necessary: a few neurons often suffice, and in many chains disjoint subsets each flip the answer on their own, in an exploratory analysis most often when the model is less confident. Group effects transfer to rephrasings of the same chain but are much weaker on other tested chains. We study neuron-level causal interventions and alternative subsets; we do not recover the full connectivity of circuits.

item.title: Saccadic Remapping in Dynamic Road Scenes
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: SocArXiv
Benjamin Wolfe et al.
Saccadic remapping enables a stable perception of the world by providing precise information about the targeted region of a planned fixation, prior to the start of a saccade to the location. During remapping, some visual neurons respond to the location of the future fixation prior to saccade onset, moving the receptive field to include the predicted fixation area before the eyes move (Duhamel et al., 1992). Previous work with static stimuli showed that, compared to covert attention, remapping provides more detailed information (Golomb, 2019). Furthermore, although remapping provides less information than fixating on a target, it is object-selective rather than based on lower-level features (Wolfe & Whitney, 2015). This suggests that input from saccadic remapping impacts perception even when the target object is never fixated. However, it is unclear whether saccadic remapping input improves spatial precision in complex and dynamic situations. Current understanding of saccadic remapping maintains that both feature level and object level, visual precision is improved by remapping at and around the location of the planned fixation. Perception of features such as shape (Harrison & Bex, 2014) and motion direction (Turi & Burr, 2012) improve in saccadic remapping. Object level perception is also improved in remapped locations (Wolfe & Whitney, 2015), suggesting that object level processing occurs for pre-saccadic information, providing a more informative perceptual representation of the visual world post-saccade. Additionally, studies on feature motion perception during remapping (He et al., 2017) suggest that motion information is gathered during saccade planning and allows for trans-saccadic continuity in the representation of object locations. This suggests remapping of motion features at target location prior to fixation. Thus, remapping information prior to the saccade itself might provide an expected motion path of a moving object during the saccade, resulting in an informative and stable representation of features post-saccade. Finally, studies have shown that improved perception does not occur only at the exact position of a future fixation, but to a lesser degree, in areas around it (He et al., 2018). As the information gathered during saccadic remapping is not limited to saccade targets, it suggests a larger receptive field change to around the future fixation rather than limited processing of a single object or location at the predicted fixation area. However, it is unclear whether the gathered information remains informative when the saccade target is part of a complex and dynamic scene rather than simple features. While extensive research on remapping has been undertaken in both human observers and non-human primates, all of this work to date has used either static or simple stimuli. Here, we will use a set of dynamic, consequential, natural scenes to probe questions in remapping in a real-world context. Specifically, we will use the Road Hazard Stimuli (Song et al., 2023), and adapt existing hazard localization tasks (Gillies & Kosovicheva, 2025), as a tool to probe saccadic remapping in a dynamic scene context. Hazard localization in dynamic scenes is a complex task, requiring both scene perception and comprehension of changes in individual objects in the scene. While hazard detection in a driving context can be supported by peripheral vision of a static road scene (Huestegge & Böckler, 2016), precise localization in a dynamic scene is likely to benefit from looking directly at potential hazards, which requires the driver to plan a saccade towards that object under time pressure and with little allowance for failure. Saccadic remapping towards potential hazards might, therefore, provide more detailed information about potential hazards prior to fixation and allow for earlier response planning. Additionally, predictive motion remapping, if applicable to objects rather than individual features, might provide additional information on the likely location of potential hazards in spite of the information loss during the saccade. Finally, if saccadic remapping provides detailed information of regions surrounding the target location, it could help estimate potential hazard locations even if they are not exactly at the targeted location. The current study will investigate how hazard localization in a real-world dynamic road scene is affected by saccadic remapping towards the scene compared to covert attention, and fixation on the scene. It will also examine how the improvement in precision varies across time points in the video (for example, whether it is limited to the time of hazard onset or a specific amount of time prior to the onset of the hazard). Predictive motion transfer during saccades might benefit localization before hazard onset, as motion prediction could provide information about objects’ position and relevance (e.g., whether or not it will genuinely be a risk) later in the video, while the detailed information provided by a saccade might improve localization. Previous studies showing that saccadic remapping improves perceptual precision (He et al., 2017) as well as processing at the object level (Wolfe & Whitney, 2015), support the idea that object localization benefits from saccadic remapping. This study will aim to quantify the increase in precision with saccadic remapping in a hazard localization task using videos of dynamic, near-collision road scenes as compared to covert attention and fixation. It will further identify the utility of saccadic remapping at different moments around hazard onset by comparing localization precision at different moments at or prior-to hazard onset.

item.title: Temporal Dynamics of Multi-Item Working Memory Maintenance in Human Gaze Patterns and EEG
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Broehl, F., Bielefeldt, A. A., Linde-Domingo, J., Spitzer, B.
Maintaining multiple items in working memory (WM) requires the allocation of limited resources, which may involve prioritizing individual items over others. Previous work has suggested that attentional prioritization can vary rhythmically between WM samples, but direct empirical evidence for such temporal fluctuations remains scarce. Here, we recorded eye-tracking and EEG to track the temporal dynamics of multi-item processing while participants maintained up to three object orientations in WM. Whereas EEG encoding was only short-lived, miniature gaze patterns reflected the orientations of all three items throughout the entire WM delay and showed systematic load and serial position effects. Contrary to rhythmic sampling accounts, however, we found no evidence that eye movements alternated between the concurrently maintained items. Furthermore, the strength of WM encoding in gaze was not modulated by frontal theta activity in EEG, suggesting that oculomotor encoding was not directly coupled to rhythmic neural dynamics associated with WM and internal attention. Together, our findings indicate that the oculomotor signature of visuospatial WM processing was rather stably shaped by all of the simultaneously maintained items. The results further corroborate that eye-tracking and EEG provide complementary windows into the temporal dynamics of WM.

item.title: Phase-specific stimulation of prefrontal beta oscillations modulates distinct cognitive processes
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Wischnewski, M., Gueth, M. R., Alekseichuk, I., Opitz, A.
Oscillatory phase has been proposed to organize neural information processing, but whether endogenous phase can be leveraged to causally shape human cognition remains unclear. Here, we tested whether repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) delivered at specific phases of endogenous beta oscillations over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex modulates working memory and response inhibition. Participants received EEG phase-controlled, closed-loop rTMS delivered at either the peak or trough of their endogenous beta rhythm, using each participant's dominant beta frequency (20-30 Hz). A conventional 20-Hz rTMS delivered independently of the beta phase served as an active control. Compared to this control and each other, peak-targeted rTMS improved response inhibition, whereas trough-targeted rTMS improved working memory. Both phase-specific behavioral effects were accompanied by corresponding increases in event-related potentials, which were not observed after conventional stimulation. Across participants, behavioral improvements correlated with stimulation-induced electrophysiological changes. Finally, phase-specific rTMS induced distinct DLPFC network expansions that complemented the behavioral effects: peak stimulation enhanced posterior centro-parietal connectivity for inhibitory control, while trough stimulation expanded anterior prefrontal networks for working memory. These findings provide first evidence that opposite phases of endogenous prefrontal beta oscillations coordinate distinct cognitive and neural processes. This establishes prefrontal beta phase as a causal dimension for shaping executive function and as a target for prefrontal rTMS to modulate cognition and non-invasively probe phase-dependent brain function.

item.title: Attention to Actions - a Visual Search Task
item.description:
Relevance: 24% | Source: SocArXiv
Angelika Lingnau et al.
Visual attention is critical for selecting relevant information from the environment and guiding behavior (Treisman, 1969). During visual search, attention determines which elements of a display are processed to identify a target. Search for a single feature can often occur in parallel, whereas search for a conjunction of multiple features typically requires serial attention (Treisman & Gelade, 1980). Previous studies using object-based visual search paradigms have shown that search performance is influenced by display size and target presence, and that identification of the target often proceeds in a serial manner across the visual field (Belke et al., 2008). The present study investigates whether these basic visual search effects extend to the recognition of human actions. Participants search for a cued locomotion action (climbing, jumping, running, or walking) among multiple static avatar images. Display size (4 vs. 8 items) and target presence (present vs. absent) are manipulated. Reaction times and eye movements are recorded to characterize attentional allocation during search. The primary goal of the study is to test whether display-size effects and differences between target-present and target-absent trials observed in object-based search also apply when people search for human actions depicted as static images.
